steps.step_body:
Welcome to your AP US History Argumentation Portfolio project! Over the course of this project, you will evolve into a historian by building a professional-grade research portfolio. You’ll be selecting and analyzing primary sources, drafting a complex thesis-driven essay, and reflecting on your growth as a scholar. By the end, you’ll have a 1,500-word Document-Based Question (DBQ) essay that evaluates the major themes of continuity and change in American history. 

We are starting our journey at the very beginning of the American story. Having just explored the regional environments of pre-contact societies and the labor transitions in the early British colonies (from indentured servitude to racialized slavery), your first task is to build a Sourcing Analysis Matrix. This matrix will house the 'raw materials' for your future essay. In this stage, you will select three documents that represent the diverse perspectives of the colonial era—Native, European, or Enslaved—and perform a deep-dive analysis on their origins.

metadata.response_instruction: Submit the titles of your three selected primary sources along with a brief explanation for each choice. Good work identifies documents that clearly represent different social, economic, or environmental perspectives of the era.

steps.step_body:
To build a strong historical argument, you need diverse voices. For your initial matrix, you must select three primary sources from the pre-contact or colonial eras (1491–1754). Look for documents that highlight the themes we discussed in class: perhaps a description of Pueblo irrigation, a Haudenosaunee oral tradition, a Virginia planter’s diary regarding the headright system, or a legal code establishing racialized slavery. 

At this stage, simply identify your three choices. For each, provide the title of the document and a one-sentence explanation of why you chose it to represent a specific colonial perspective.

Now that you have your documents, it's time to apply the HIPP method of analysis—the gold standard for AP History. For each document, you need to identify its Historical Context (what was happening at the time?), Intended Audience (who was this written for?), Purpose (why was it created?), and Point of View (how does the author's background shape the message?). 

Focus on your first document today. Draft a thorough analysis that moves beyond simple summaries. For example, if you are analyzing a Virginia Slave Code, don't just say it's about laws; explain how it was a response to the elite's fear of united labor after Bacon's Rebellion. Use this step to draft the HIPP components for all three of your selected documents.

metadata.response_instruction: Upload your initial Sourcing Analysis Matrix as a PDF. Your matrix must include three distinct primary sources with a complete HIPP analysis for each. Criteria for success: accurate historical context, clear identification of the author's perspective, and a professional, organized layout.

steps.step_body:
It's time to formalize your research. You will now submit your completed Primary Source Selection and Sourcing Analysis Matrix. This matrix should be a clean, organized document where each of your three sources is listed alongside its full HIPP analysis (Historical Context, Intended Audience, Purpose, and Point of View). 

This matrix is the foundation of your portfolio. Make sure your 'Point of View' analysis specifically addresses how the author's social or economic position—like being a wealthy planter or a displaced native—influenced the way they recorded history.

Great work completing the first stage of your portfolio! You now have three deeply analyzed pieces of evidence that you can use to build a complex historical argument. Take a moment to look at your three documents together: do they tell a story of conflict, cooperation, or change? 

In our next stage, we will expand this matrix with five more sources from later periods of American history to see how these colonial foundations evolved over time. Keep your matrix handy, as it will be the primary source of evidence for your upcoming essay outline.

stages.stage_title: Primary Source Selection and Sourcing Analysis Matrix
stages.stage_description: Select three historical documents representing different colonial perspectives and complete a systematic sourcing analysis (historical context, intended audience, purpose, and point of view) for each.
stages.deliverable_increment: An initial sourcing analysis matrix containing three fully annotated primary documents from the pre-contact and colonial eras.

steps.step_body: In the previous stages, you analyzed primary sources from the colonial era and explored the shifting dynamics of power following the Seven Years' War. You have seen how 'Salutary Neglect' dissolved into a constitutional crisis over representation and how the American states experimented with their own constitutions during the war. Now, it is time to move from analysis to synthesis. In this stage, you will begin building the skeleton of your DBQ essay by formulating a complex thesis and a structured outline that tracks these changes in governance and identity from the colonial period through the drafting of the U.S. Constitution.

metadata.response_instruction: Submit a short paragraph identifying two historical developments and explaining the tension between liberty and order. A good response will show how one event prioritized local/individual rights and the other prioritized centralized stability.

steps.step_body: A strong AP-style argument requires identifying a 'tension' or 'complexity.' Consider the contrast between the weak federal structure of the Articles of Confederation and the stronger central government proposed by the Federalists. Think about how the concept of 'Republican Motherhood' expanded educational roles for women while maintaining traditional gender hierarchies. Before drafting your thesis, choose two specific historical developments from our recent sessions (e.g., the transition from the Stamp Act to the Constitution, or the radical vs. conservative state constitutions) and explain in 2-3 sentences how they represent a conflict between 'liberty' and 'order.'

metadata.response_instruction: Submit your drafted thesis statement. A high-scoring thesis will avoid being a simple 'yes/no' and will instead use transition words (like 'while', 'however', or 'although') to demonstrate an understanding of both continuity and change.

steps.step_body: Now, draft your thesis statement. Remember that a complex thesis should acknowledge multiple perspectives, often using the 'Although [X], [Y] because [A and B]' formula. Your thesis must address the extent to which the American Revolution and the subsequent move toward the Constitution changed American governance and identity. It should be defensible, meaning someone could argue against it, and it must set the stage for the thematic categories you will use in your essay.

With your thesis as your 'North Star,' you must now build the structural framework of your essay. Create an analytical outline that organizes your argument into three thematic body paragraphs (e.g., Political Sovereignty, Social Identity, or Federal Power). For each paragraph, include a clear topic sentence that links back to your thesis. Under each topic sentence, list specific historical evidence you will use, such as the Federalist Papers, the Articles of Confederation, or state constitutional models like Pennsylvania (1776) or Massachusetts (1780).

metadata.response_instruction: Upload a PDF of your formal essay outline. The outline must include: 1) Your complex thesis statement, 2) Three thematic topic sentences, and 3) At least two specific pieces of historical evidence (proper nouns/events/documents) per body paragraph that illustrate change or continuity.

steps.step_body: Review your outline to ensure your evidence is placed logically and that your topic sentences directly support the complex thesis you drafted earlier. This document serves as the roadmap for your final 1,500-word DBQ essay, so ensure the connection between your documents and your historical claims is clear.

You've successfully moved from analyzing individual documents to creating a cohesive historical argument. In the next stage, we will begin the actual drafting process, where you will weave your primary source matrix directly into this outline. Keep your outline handy, as it will be the blueprint for your writing.

stages.stage_title: Formulating a Complex Thesis Statement and Historical Outline
stages.stage_description: Draft a defensible, multi-perspective thesis statement addressing changes in governance and identity from the colonial era through the Constitutional Convention. Create an analytical outline that structures these arguments into thematic body paragraphs.
stages.deliverable_increment: A formal, structured essay outline featuring a complex thesis statement, targeted topic sentences, and specific historical evidence alignments (such as the Articles of Confederation and Federalist Papers).

steps.step_body: In the previous stages, you analyzed colonial-era documents and drafted a complex thesis statement that tracked federal versus state power through the early republic. You also recently explored how 'Manifest Destiny' and the Mexican-American War reignited the toxic debate over slavery's expansion. Now, it is time to move from planning to execution. In this stage, you will bridge your early-republic analysis with the ideological fractures of the Civil War and Reconstruction eras to draft your full 1,500-word argumentative essay. Your goal is to show how definitions of citizenship and federal authority didn't just change, but were radically redefined by the conflict.

metadata.response_instruction: Provide a 3-5 sentence explanation of how you will integrate the economic dependence on cotton and 'Free Soil' ideology as external historical evidence. Good work will specifically connect these economic factors to the political breakdown of the Second Party System.

steps.step_body: Before you begin drafting your body paragraphs, look at the economic drivers we discussed in Session 4.1.3. Review the 'King Cotton' flow chart and how it fueled the expansion of slavery into the Deep South. Consider how this economic reality clashed with the 'Free Soil' ideology of the North. In a few sentences, explain how you will use this economic conflict as 'outside evidence' (evidence not found in the documents) to support your argument about the inevitability of sectional conflict.

metadata.response_instruction: Submit a drafted topic sentence for a body paragraph. It should clearly link a specific ideological shift (e.g., Compact Theory vs. Perpetual Union) to your overall thesis about the evolution of federal power.

steps.step_body: Now, focus on the transition from the 'Compact Theory' to the 'Perpetual Union' stance discussed in Session 4.2.1. Your essay must evaluate how the Civil War fundamentally altered the balance of power. Think about Lincoln’s maneuver at Fort Sumter or the ideological shift from slavery as a 'necessary evil' to a 'positive good.' Choose one of these specific historical shifts and draft a topic sentence for a body paragraph that connects this shift back to your core thesis on federal power.

metadata.response_instruction: Upload your complete 1,500-word first draft as a PDF. Criteria for success: 1) A clear, complex thesis in the introduction; 2) Integration and analysis of 6+ primary sources; 3) Use of specific historical context (e.g., Wilmot Proviso, Anaconda Plan, or Reconstruction amendments); 4) A logical argument that tracks changes in citizenship or federal power.

steps.step_body: It is time to assemble your full draft. Using your previously created outline and source matrix, write your 1,500-word essay. You must integrate at least 6 primary sources, ensuring you explain how the sourcing (Point of View, Purpose, Historical Situation, or Audience) of at least 3 of them supports your argument. Be sure to weave in the Civil War and Reconstruction content we covered, specifically addressing how the definition of citizenship changed for formerly enslaved people and how the federal government’s role expanded during and after the war.

metadata.response_instruction: Type a brief reflection (100-200 words) identifying two documents you struggled to synthesize and explaining the historical or logical tension between them.

steps.step_body: Writing a long-form historical argument is a major milestone. To wrap up this stage, look back at your draft and identify which two documents were the most difficult to synthesize into a single argument. Why was it challenging to make them 'talk' to each other? Reflecting on these friction points will help you refine your logic during the final polishing stage of the portfolio.

stages.stage_title: Synthesizing Evidence and Writing the Core Argumentative Essay Draft
stages.stage_description: Combine your prior historical outlines and source analyses to draft a comprehensive, multi-paragraph historical argument. Integrate new evidence from the Civil War and Reconstruction eras to evaluate how definitions of citizenship and federal power evolved over time.
stages.deliverable_increment: A complete first draft of your 1,500-word historical essay, integrating analysis of at least 6 primary sources and incorporating external historical evidence.

steps.step_body: Welcome to the final stage of your AP US History portfolio! Over the past units, you have analyzed early colonial documents, outlined a complex argument, and drafted a 1,500-word essay that synthesizes historical evidence. Now, it is time to bring these pieces together. Review your previous work, particularly your essay draft and your initial sourcing matrix. Your goal today is to polish these components into a professional, cohesive portfolio that tracks a central historical theme across the full span of American history, ensuring your narrative reaches into the modern era of the Cold War and Civil Rights.

metadata.response_instruction: Submit a 3-5 sentence explanation of how you will modify your essay to include more complexity, specifically referencing a modern historical development (like the Cold War or Civil Rights) discussed in recent sessions.

steps.step_body: A high-scoring AP essay must demonstrate 'complexity'—this means you shouldn't just argue one side, but instead show how patterns of continuity and change coexist. Review your current draft. Does it address how the themes of federal power or civil rights changed during the Cold War era? Reflecting on our recent lessons, consider how the Truman Doctrine or the Civil Rights Movement's shift from legalism to Black Power adds a new layer to your argument. Write a brief explanation of where you plan to add or refine a paragraph to better demonstrate this historical complexity.

metadata.response_instruction: Upload your completed 8-document Sourcing Analysis Matrix. Good work shows a deep understanding of the 'HIPP' elements for each source and includes a variety of document types across multiple centuries.

steps.step_body: Your portfolio requires an annotated primary source matrix analyzing 8 diverse documents. In earlier stages, you completed the first three documents from the colonial era. Now, complete the remaining five entries. Ensure these documents span different eras and perspectives, such as the Federalist Papers, the Truman Doctrine, or King’s 'Letter from Birmingham Jail.' For each, you must identify the historical situation, intended audience, purpose, and point of view (HIPP analysis).

metadata.response_instruction: Submit a short self-reflection (2 paragraphs). The first should identify your strongest evidence use, and the second should describe a specific change you made to better align your essay with the AP DBQ rubric.

steps.step_body: Before the final submission, you must think like an AP grader. Use the official AP DBQ rubric to evaluate your 1,500-word essay. Specifically, look for: 1) a clear, defensible thesis; 2) effective use of at least 6 sources; 3) inclusion of 'outside evidence' (historical facts not found in the documents); and 4) a sophisticated argument that accounts for historical nuance. Identify one specific area where your essay is strongest and one area where you made a final improvement to meet these standards.

metadata.response_instruction: Upload your final AP US History Argumentation Portfolio as a single PDF. A complete submission includes the polished essay, the full 8-source matrix, and the self-reflection sheet. Criteria for success: academic tone, mastery of historical context, and a clear, complex argumentative thread throughout.

steps.step_body: It is time to submit your masterwork. Combine your polished 1,500-word essay, your 8-document sourcing matrix, and your self-evaluation into a single comprehensive AP US History Argumentation Portfolio. This collection represents your journey from raw primary source analysis to a sophisticated, historical argument that mirrors the rigor of an AP exam. Double-check that your citations are consistent and your thesis is prominently placed in the introduction.

Congratulations on completing a massive undertaking! You have successfully tracked a historical theme through over 500 years of change and continuity. By synthesizing documents from the founding of the nation to the heights of the Cold War and the struggle for Civil Rights, you've demonstrated the skills of a professional historian. Take a moment to consider how your understanding of American identity or power has evolved by looking at these documents as a single, connected story.

stages.stage_title: Peer-Style Review and Final Argumentation Portfolio Assembly
stages.stage_description: Refine your historical essay by expanding the context to the modern era, verifying that your arguments demonstrate historical complexity (such as discussing both continuity and change). Complete a self-evaluation against official AP DBQ writing rubrics.
stages.deliverable_increment: The finalized AP US History Argumentation Portfolio, including the polished 1,500-word essay, the 8-document sourcing matrix, and a detailed self-evaluation reflection sheet.

projects.project_name: AP US History Document-Based Essay and Historical Argumentation Portfolio
projects.final_deliverable: A comprehensive 4-part AP US History Argumentation Portfolio consisting of: 1) a annotated primary source matrix analyzing 8 diverse historical documents; 2) an essay outline with a complex, thesis-driven roadmap; 3) a fully-drafted 1,500-word Document-Based Question (DBQ) essay evaluating continuity and change in American history; and 4) a self-grading rubric reflection aligning with AP history thinking standards.
projects.project_description: Throughout this course, you will build a comprehensive, academic AP-style historical analysis portfolio. You will select, analyze, and synthesize primary and secondary sources to construct a highly rigorous, evidence-based Document-Based Essay (DBQ) that tracks a central historical theme—such as the evolution of federal power versus states' rights, or the expansion of civil rights—across American history from 1491 to the present.
